history.heading: The Helen of the West Indies
paragraphs: Saint Lucia, a volcanic island in the eastern Caribbean, was inhabited by Arawak and then Kalinago peoples, who resisted early European settlement. France and Britain fought over the island for over 150 years, and it changed hands 14 times, earning it the nickname "Helen of the West Indies".
Britain gained permanent control in 1814. Sugar plantations used enslaved Africans until slavery was abolished in 1834.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: Saint Lucia became independent on 22 February 1979. It has produced two Nobel laureates, more per person than any other country: economist Sir Arthur Lewis (1979) and poet Derek Walcott (1992).

culture.heading: Creole heritage
paragraphs: English is official, and Saint Lucian Kwéyòl, a French-based Creole, is widely spoken. Most people are Catholic. Jounen Kwéyòl (Creole Day) celebrates local culture, and the Saint Lucia Jazz Festival is popular. Green fig (green banana) and saltfish is the national dish. The Pitons, two volcanic spires, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

politics.heading: Parliamentary democracy
paragraphs: Saint Lucia is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm with the British monarch represented by a governor-general. The Saint Lucia Labour Party and the United Workers Party are the main parties.

economy.heading: Tourism
paragraphs: Tourism is the main source of income, with luxury resorts and cruise visitors. Banana exports, once dominant, have declined. Offshore finance and a citizenship-by-investment programme also contribute. The currency is the Eastern Caribbean dollar.
